title: Teaching
text:
Thesis supervision
I supervise theses that use quantitative or computational methods on questions about political communication and behaviour. Topics I am well placed to supervise include:

Political advertising and microtargeting on social platforms
Misinformation, AI-generated content, and how audiences evaluate it
Politicians’ and parties’ communication strategies
Comment sections and online political discussion
Descriptive and measurement-focused projects on Danish politics

A good starting point is a question you can actually get data on. If you are unsure whether that is the case for your idea, bring it to office hours — that is often the fastest way to find out.

title: Media & outreach
text:
I spend a good deal of time communicating research beyond the journals — both my own findings and small-scale descriptive analyses that are useful to the public and to journalists. Since 2022 I have commented on digital platforms’ role in society more than 50 times across Danish news media, on topics from online political microtargeting to the influence of misinformation and AI-generated content.
The research has also been picked up by lawmakers and organisations: it features in DR’s strategy, and I have written for the Danish Ministry of Digitalisation.

title: Mads Fuglsang Hove
text:
Assistant Professor · Department of Political Science, Aarhus University

I am a computational social scientist working at the intersection of communication science, political science, and data science. My research asks how digital media affects contemporary democracy: how political actors — politicians, parties, and media outlets — communicate strategically on digital platforms, and how citizens respond to what reaches them, from online misinformation and AI-generated content to the discussions unfolding in comment sections.
I hold a PhD in Communication Science from the University of Amsterdam, completed in affiliation with the Digital Democracy Centre at the University of Southern Denmark.
Read about my research Publications

title: Mads Fuglsang Hove
text:
Approach
Methodologically, I collect and analyse large social media datasets through platforms’ research APIs, and combine text-as-data methods with LLM-based content classification, survey research, and (field) experiments.
I take measurement seriously. Alongside systematic descriptive work, I develop new measures — for instance a targeting ideology measure that infers political elites’ perceptions of voter groups from the way they target online advertisements. I work primarily in R and particularly enjoy data visualisation.

title: Research
text: My work asks how digital media reshape the relationship between political elites and citizens. Three strands run through it: how elites target and communicate, what citizens are able to tell about the content that reaches them, and how elite media strategy translates into public standing. A fourth, newer strand looks at what happens in the discussions themselves.

title: Research
text:
Political microtargeting


Elite strategy

Online political advertising lets parties address different voter groups with different messages, largely out of public view. My dissertation, The Nature and Consequences of Online Political Microtargeting, asks what parties actually do with that capacity and what follows from it.
Rather than treating targeting as a black box, I use the targeting criteria parties themselves select as data. This yields a targeting ideology measure: an inference about how political elites perceive and sort the electorate, drawn from their own advertising choices. Across multi-party systems, the pattern that emerges is less sophisticated persuasion of swing voters than reinforcement of existing constituencies — parties largely preach to their own choirs.
The work is comparative as well as Danish: with colleagues I have mapped microtargeting usage worldwide, documenting how unevenly the practice is distributed across countries and party families.

title: Research
text:
AI-generated content and misinformation


Citizen responses

Generative AI has made synthetic images cheap and abundant. A basic democratic question follows: can people tell? In large-scale studies with colleagues from Copenhagen, Aarhus, and SDU, we find that most people cannot reliably distinguish AI-generated images from photographs — detection accuracy sits far closer to chance than most people assume of themselves.
This line of work connects to a broader interest in the role of digital platforms in the information environment, which I have also written about for the Danish Ministry of Digitalisation.

title: Research
section: Elite media strategy and public standing
text:
Elite media strategy and public standing


Elites and the public

Politicians invest heavily in visibility. Does it pay? Working with Danish ministers, I examine how media activity relates to public approval and name recognition — and for whom that effort registers. The answer is not uniform across the electorate, which raises questions about who the audience for political communication effectively is.

title: Research
text:
Online political discussion


Work in progress

Comment sections under posts from politicians and news outlets are one of the few places where elites and citizens meet in public. I am currently working on what these discussions look like from both sides: how politicians manage and moderate the spaces they open, and what draws citizens into them.

title: Research
text:
Methods
I collect and analyse large social media datasets through platforms’ research APIs and combine several approaches depending on the question:

Text-as-data and LLM-based classification for large corpora of political messages and comments
Survey research and (field) experiments for questions about citizen perception and effects
Descriptive and measurement work — systematically documenting phenomena that are often asserted but rarely measured, and building new indicators where none exist

Nearly all of it happens in R.
